responses: Pneumonia is an infection or inflammation of the lungs that affects the tiny air sacs (alveoli) where oxygen exchange happens.
When those air sacs become inflamed, they may fill with fluid or inflammatory material, so breathing can feel harder and oxygen transfer can drop.
Common symptoms can include cough (sometimes with phlegm), fever or chills, tiredness, chest discomfort, and shortness of breath—but symptoms vary by person and cause.
Not every cough is pneumonia, and not every pneumonia looks the same. Symptoms can overlap with colds or flu, especially early on.
High-level causes can include viruses, bacteria, or aspiration (breathing in food/liquid). Symptoms alone usually cannot confirm the cause.
Clinicians diagnose pneumonia using the overall picture: history, exam (listening to lungs), vital signs, and sometimes a chest X-ray or labs.
Home care may be reasonable only when symptoms are mild and stable; worsening symptoms should trigger medical review.
Emergency warning signs include severe breathing trouble, blue/gray lips, confusion, fainting, or severe chest pain—call emergency services immediately.

responses: Pneumonia treatment depends on severity, age, and medical history—so clinicians tailor the plan rather than using one universal approach.
Antibiotics are used only when a clinician suspects or confirms a bacterial cause; they do not treat viral pneumonia directly.

Supportive care is important in most cases and may include:
- Rest and pacing activity
- Fluids to avoid dehydration
- Comfort measures for fever and aches (follow product labels and your clinician’s advice)
- Monitoring breathing and overall trend
Some people need in-person monitoring, oxygen support, or hospital care when breathing is difficult, oxygen is low, or symptoms are severe.
Do not self-prescribe antibiotics, use leftovers, or take someone else’s prescription—this can be unsafe and may delay correct care.
If a clinician prescribes medication, take it exactly as directed and contact them if side effects or worsening symptoms occur.
Follow-up matters if you are not improving, if symptoms return after brief improvement, or if you are in a higher-risk group.

responses: Prevention focuses on lowering your risk of respiratory infections and reducing the chance they become severe.

Vaccines can help reduce severe illness from infections that may lead to pneumonia. Which vaccines are recommended depends on age, health conditions, and local guidance—so a clinician is the best source for what applies to you.

Common prevention steps include:
- Staying up to date on recommended vaccines (based on your clinician’s guidance)
- Frequent hand hygiene
- Avoiding close contact when you or others are sick
- Covering coughs/sneezes and improving ventilation
- Avoiding smoking and secondhand smoke exposure
Vaccines do not prevent every infection, but they can reduce severity and complications in many people.
If you are at higher risk (older adults, chronic lung/heart disease, immune compromise), preventive planning is especially important.
If you are unsure what you need, ask: “Which vaccines are recommended for me, and when?”
If you develop severe breathing symptoms despite prevention, seek urgent care—prevention is not a guarantee.
Use trusted public-health sources for current recommendations in your region.

- Blue/gray lips or face
